source.title: The semantic landscape paradigm for neural networks

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses neural scaling laws and derives theoretical scaling forms for its own fallibility construct, but it does not measure or test held-out language-model loss, extrapolation, or compute-optimal allocation.
record.gate_note: The scaling-law results are theoretical predictions for fallibility F in the semantic trap model. The paper explicitly distinguishes fallibility from measured test loss. Empirical results attributed to cited studies are not recorded as this paper's results.
record.test_reason: Purely theoretical paper: it derives power-law forms for 'fallibility' (a KL divergence over all possible inputs, stated to be distinct from measured test loss) under an assumed semantic trap model. It reports no measurement of language-model loss, no fits, no extrapolation, no allocation, architecture or downstream results. Its only numbers (µ≈0.1) are back-fitted from Kaplan et al.'s cited exponent, not from its own runs. An explanatory theory is not a test of any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The author proposes the semantic landscape paradigm as a unifying framework: grokking and emergence with scale are percolation transitions, and scaling laws follow from random-walk and trap statistics. Matching Kaplan's data exponent gives µ≈0.1, likened to glassy aging. The paper is presented as an incipient, phenomenological theory to be developed with mechanistic interpretability.
record.recipe_differences: The paper proposes a theoretical framework rather than reproducing the original scaling-law experiments or their measurement recipe.
record.method_sensitivity: The predicted parameter-count exponent depends on µ, df, and α; the dataset-size and training-time exponents are µ in the stated model. The derivations also use different limiting regimes for D and N.

fits_no_version.finding: Semantic trap model predicts fallibility power laws in training steps, parameters and data. It predicts identical exponents for data and training time (both µ), and an N exponent µ/(df α).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Theoretical claim: barrier-crossing dynamics on a graph of learned algorithms yield power-law scaling with equal data and time exponents.

record.problems: The scaling results are theoretical and depend on phenomenological assumptions, including the exponential barrier distribution and the relation between fallibility and barrier crossings. No empirical validation of these predictions is reported in this paper, and fallibility is not the measured test loss.
record.rows_left_out: No results from cited studies were included; they are literature context rather than results of this paper. No held-out-loss, extrapolation, architecture, compute-optimal allocation, or downstream-task outcomes are reported by the paper itself.

untested.parts: No held-out loss measured; only theoretical fallibility power laws in S, N, D derived.
No small-run fits or predictions of larger runs.
No compute-optimal allocation analysis; compute is not modelled.
No other modalities or regimes tested; the claimed generality is only asserted.
No downstream tasks measured; emergence is discussed as percolation, qualitatively.
Exponents depend on model parameters µ, df, α in theory; no empirical fitting-choice comparison.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's T6/discusses classification is correct. An alternative would be 'cites_only/discusses' with T6. No empirical results; the µ≈0.1 value comes from matching cited Kaplan et al. exponents, not from this paper's own data. Rows could be dropped as non-results, but they are kept with versions ['none'].

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining loss is measured; the derivations concern fallibility under model assumptions.
No small-run fits or predictions of larger-run losses are evaluated.
No fixed-compute allocation between parameter count and tokens is evaluated.
No architecture comparison at fixed parameter count is reported.
No scaling-law results are tested across modalities or training regimes.
No downstream task performance is measured; the discussion of its relation to loss cites other work.
The paper does not test the effects of fitting choices, data, or training schedules on empirical exponents, or measure departures from power-law curves.
